overview.text: The unemployment rate, also called the jobless rate, measures unemployed people as a percentage of the labor force—not the entire population. In the U.S. official measure, the labor force consists of employed people plus those counted as unemployed. A jobless person generally must be available for work and have actively searched in the previous four weeks; people on temporary layoff awaiting recall are an exception. The rate is calculated as unemployed ÷ labor force × 100. Economists and policymakers watch it as an indicator of labor-market conditions, but it is not a complete picture: people who want work but recently stopped searching, and people working part time who want full-time work, are not fully captured by the headline rate.

key_facts.text: The labor force is the sum of employed and unemployed people; it is the denominator in the rate.

In the U.S. Current Population Survey, unemployed people generally had no job, were available for work, and actively searched during the prior four weeks. People awaiting recall from temporary layoff need not have searched.
The BLS calls its official unemployment measure U-3.
People who want and are available for work but have not actively searched in the last four weeks—including discouraged workers—are not counted as unemployed in the official measure.
The broader U-6 measure also includes marginally attached people and people working part time for economic reasons.
